children: By Emmanuel Bruce
Ghana's cocoa buyers are owed about 4 billion cedi ($349 million) by regulator COCOBOD for last season's crop, and want it paid before the new crop year begins, an industry body told Reuters.
The Chamber of Cocoa Marketers, which represents Ghana's licensed cocoa buyers, also warned that financing may not yet be in place to fund purchases when the season opens.

"Up till now, we have not seen any visible or reliable funding to show that COCOBOD is prepared for the opening, but we need money and a lot of it to be able to buy cocoa,” its CEO Vitus Dzah said in an interview.
COCOBOD did not respond to a request for comment.
Licensed buyers are an early link in Ghana's cocoa supply chain, purchasing beans from farmers and supplying them to COCOBOD, which sells them on to processors and international traders.
COCOBOD YET TO TELL BUYERS WHEN NEW SEASON WILL BEGIN
Ghana and Ivory Coast, the world's two biggest cocoa producers, agreed to harmonize their farmgate prices and season start dates after a meeting between the countries' presidents in June.
But COCOBOD has yet to communicate to licensed buyers when the new season will begin, even though Ivory Coast opened its season on September 1.

The regulator usually secures funds before opening the season, but it has struggled to finance cocoa purchases since a decades-old syndicated loan arrangement with international banks collapsed during the 2023/24 season.
A separate arrangement under which international trading houses pre-financed purchases fell through last season, contributing to delays in payments to farmers.

In an interview with local radio on Tuesday, COCOBOD's head of public affairs Jerome Sam said the arrears were part of a routine reimbursement cycle and that licensed buyers could pre-finance cocoa purchases with COCOBOD reimbursing them later, as has happened in recent years.
COCOBOD plans to meet with licensed buyers to resolve outstanding payments, Sam said, without providing details.
"All the necessary actions and decisions have almost come to an end, and we are hoping the government will soon announce the opening of the season," he said.
REGULATOR EXPLORES LOCAL BRIDGE FINANCING, SOURCES SAY

Dzah told Reuters that COCOBOD was not required to fund licensed buying companies directly, as they must demonstrate their own funding capacity to obtain a license, but needed to secure and ring-fence its own financing so buyers can be paid promptly for cocoa delivered.

“We are saying that COCOBOD must get its funding ready and ring-fenced so that if we go out there and buy cocoa and deliver, there will be real-time payment for us to go back and then buy again,” he said.
COCOBOD has been exploring raising about 2 billion cedi in bridge financing on the local market, sources familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Two pension fund sources and one bank source said lead arrangers contacted them last month about the facility, but had not followed up since.

COCOBOD’s CEO Ransford Abbey told local media last month that the board planned to raise money through local bonds and commercial paper in August, while the finance minister has previously said COCOBOD would issue local bonds in three tranches targeting pension funds and banks.
($1 = 11.4700 Ghanian cedi)
